1:
The opening is a man talking to himself, and every reader notices it. Henry says he is no fool who thus talks to himself and excites his own soul to good, and that we make nothing of religious performances unless we make heart-work of them. Calvin turns the same observation into a rebuke of the reader. The prophet teaches every man by his example; and if one inflamed with a more fervent zeal than other men was not free from this malady — his earnestness in stimulating himself being a plain confession of it — how much more do we need the same remedy, that every man descend into himself and correct his own sluggishness. The repetition makes the language more emphatic still. Spurgeon gives it a phrase: soul music is the very soul of music, and the psalmist strikes the best key-note in stirring up his inmost self.

Augustine will not let all that is within me stay physical. He supposes it does not mean what is inside the body — there are lungs in our breast like a kind of bellows, and no utterance can sound from the mouth but what they give vent to, yet all that relates to the ears of men. God has ears, and the heart also has a voice; what is within is the soul itself. Let our voices bless him at intervals, but let the voice of our hearts never fall silent. Gill adds that God is to be served with the best we have, bodily exercise profiting nothing unless the spirit is engaged; and since he is all-sufficient and blessed for evermore, to bless him cannot mean conferring a blessing but proclaiming his blessedness.

On the date they divide quietly. Clarke reports that the inscription in the Hebrew and all the versions gives the psalm to David, but that many of the ancients referred it to the end of the captivity, when the redeemed gave thanks for their restoration. Delitzsch resists that: the ascription rests on tradition, since no internal ground could have produced it — though he grants the language does not favour it, the psalm having an Aramaic colouring and a heaping up of Aramaizing suffix-forms unequalled outside one narrative in Kings, which he takes for intentional ornaments, not errors.

Forgetting is the real danger. Henry holds that if we do not give thanks for mercies we forget them, which is unjust as well as unkind, and puts the reproach in the psalmist's mouth: thou hast forgotten many of his benefits, but surely not all. Clarke turns it into a method: call them into recollection, particularize the chief, record them for an everlasting memorial. Delitzsch sets the psalm against the one before, whose promise of compassion on Zion is its substance throughout. Ellicott notes that the word for benefits means simply actions, good or bad, and finds the significance in its restriction here: God's acts are all benefits. He makes forgiveness the first benefit to anyone aiming at the higher life, since God's benefits will not be before our eyes unless our sins are also; the diseases he takes chiefly morally, as the parallel with iniquity shows. Henry pairs them: our crimes were capital and our diseases mortal, and God saves our lives by pardoning the one and healing the other — the two going together, for if he takes away the guilt by pardoning mercy he will break the power by renewing grace. Gill insists on the scope of the pardon: not lesser sins but iniquities of a scarlet dye, and all of them. Clarke numbers the benefits and reads the redemption as redemption of life by the kinsman, looking forward to him who became partaker of our flesh that he might redeem us by dying in our stead. Ellicott prefers pit or grave to destruction and derives the crown from the wreaths worn on festive occasions.
5:
The eagle divides the readers most. Clarke prints his old Psalter's legend — the bird's beak growing in old age until it cannot open its mouth, whereupon it smites the beak on a stone, breaks off the excrescence and becomes young again, as Christ takes away our old age of sin — then dismisses it. There are as many legends of the eagle among the ancient writers as of some saints in the calendar, and all equally true; no small portion of them, he complains, have been crowded into comments on this verse. The psalmist means nothing more than the annual moulting common to all birds, and chose this one for its bulk, strength and long life. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the lexicon. The notion that the eagle renewed its youth was the basis of a rabbinical story and appears in the myth of the phoenix, but the psalmist refers merely to the fresh appearance of the bird in its new plumage. He also reads the first clause differently: the versions give desire and body for the word rendered mouth, but the Chaldee gives age, which the derivation supports and which yields the best sense — who satisfieth thine age with good. The bird, he adds, is properly the griffon or great vulture, eagle following the Greek.

Gill will have none of the body in it. Not the youth of the frame nor outward prosperity, but the youth of grace renewed; and the good things are the favour in God's heart, the fulness of grace in Christ's hands, and the provisions of the Lord's house, which he shows to his people, creates a hunger for, and satisfies. He reports the Greek rendering, who filleth thy desire with good things, and a Jewish reading that takes the word as an ornament and gives who satisfieth thy soul. Wesley reduces the whole to a clause: the eagle lives long in great strength and vigour.

With the sixth verse the psalm turns outward, and everyone marks it. Ellicott notes that the poet passes from individual to national mercies and goes back to the favour granted to Moses. Delitzsch says the range of vision is widened, and calls the verse a commonplace drawn from the history of Israel. Henry makes the widening a duty: the psalmist had fetched matter for praise from his own experience and now looks abroad at God's favour to others, all the saints being fed at a common table. Spurgeon says the same more sharply — our own personal obligations must not absorb our song.

The executing of judgment is then pressed in different directions. Gill widens the class of the oppressed as far as it will go: the Israelites under the Egyptians; the poor, the widow and the fatherless; good men under tyrannical princes; those oppressed by the man of sin; and those buffeted by Satan, whom the Lord delivers in his own time. Henry keeps it plainer: even in common providence God is the patron of wronged innocence and will one way or another plead the cause of the injured, since it is his honour to humble the proud and help the helpless. Spurgeon presses the other half. God is the executor of the poor and the executioner of the cruel: when his people were in Egypt he heard their groanings and brought them out, but he also overthrew Pharaoh in the sea. Mercy to the saints demands vengeance on their persecutors: no blood of martyrs is shed in vain, no groans of confessors left uninquired into. Justice may at times leave the courts of man, but it abides on the tribunal of God; were he content to let high-handed oppressors escape, we should have greater reason for trembling than rejoicing. Clarke states the balance in a sentence: he is slow to anger but will punish; he is plenteous in mercy and will save.
7:
The ways made known to Moses are read at several depths. Clarke keeps it historical: God has been our protector from the earliest part of our history, and his acts for Israel are so many reasons to trust him now. Gill goes furthest, dividing the ways into three — creation, since natural light might tell us that God made all things but never in what manner; providence, sometimes in the deep and past finding out; and grace by Christ, made known to Moses as the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head. Henry draws the lesson: revelation is the greatest favour with which the church is blessed, for God restores us to himself by revealing himself to us.

The formula that follows is recognised as a quotation. Ellicott notes that the original confession at Sinai had become a formula of the national faith; Henry makes the same connection with the proclamation of the name at the mount. Gill spreads the two adjectives across the whole order of salvation, and makes the mercy free, without motive or merit in men. Delitzsch keeps to the figures, remarking that they illustrate the unreservedness of mercy, and that the verse on the father sounds as much like the spirit of the New Testament as those before it, the relation of those who fear God being filial and freely reciprocal.

The chiding is qualified in the same direction by all. Gill allows that God does chide his children, but never except for a fault, and never for chiding's sake as some parents do; he chides for their profit and does not continue it. Clarke says he has often reproved and punished, but his mercy ever rejoiced over judgment. Both then insist on the same distinction: God deals with his people roundly for their sins, by his Spirit, his ministers and his rod, but never as those sins deserve, nor regulates his mercy by our merits.

The two measurements are then examined. Gill takes the height of heaven above earth for the greatest distance conceivable, yet calls it a faint representation of a boundless mercy; on the east and west he insists the comparison is between the opposite points of the heavens, not of the earth, which scarcely exceeds twelve thousand miles across. Clarke makes the point differently: east and west can never meet but must be for ever at the same distance, and so our sins are removed to an eternal distance. Ellicott alters the sense, rendering it not so great is his mercy but so far, above what was expected, does his mercy prevail; Wesley says the same in five words, above their deserts and expectations.

On the father and the dust the tone changes. Clarke calls the verse very emphatic and translates it as tender compassions answering tender compassions: what a father feels toward a disobedient child melted into tears, God feels in kind but infinitely more exquisitely toward the penitent. He reads the frame as our formation, the manner in which we are constructed, and lists what God takes into account: the frailty of our nature, the untowardness of our circumstances, the strength of temptation, and the party the tempter has within us. Gill hears in the word the term the Jews use for the corruption of nature, and takes the knowledge to be of both frames, the brittle ware of the body and the proneness of the mind. Henry sharpens the flower: the garden flower is choicer and lasts longer for the shelter of the wall and the gardener's care, but this is the flower of the field, withering in itself and exposed to cold blasts, liable to be cropped and trodden. God considers this and pities him; let man consider it himself. Ellicott adds the scorching eastern wind that blasts every green thing, and Gray's lines on the man missed one morning from the accustomed hill.
17:
Gill marks the antithesis: against the withering flower the psalm sets a mercy that does not wither. It reaches from one eternity to another — from everlasting in the heart of God, appearing in the choice of the vessels of mercy and in the covenant; then in time in regeneration, forgiveness, and a salvation by mercy and not by works. The fear on which it rests, he adds, is not servile but filial, a fear of the Lord and of his goodness. Clarke works the two nouns. The first signifies the exuberant goodness of God, an attribute of his nature and therefore necessarily everlasting; the second is his merciful mode of justifying the ungodly, and that is what extends to children's children — still in force, and to be preached until time ends. On the covenant Clarke gives its spirit in a sentence — I will be your God and we will be thy people — and derives the commandments from it.

The throne is where the psalm widens for the last time. Gill dwells on the fixity — a throne that cannot be moved, standing when others are cast down. Henry makes the verse the doctrine of universal providence: God secures the happiness of his peculiar people by promise and covenant, but the order of mankind in general by common providence. He that made all rules all, and both by a word of power; the throne is prepared above us and out of sight, since he holds back its face and spreads a cloud upon it, and yet he can judge through the dark cloud. Yet though he keeps his court in heaven, his kingdom rules over all kings and kingdoms, and from it there is no exempt jurisdiction. Clarke says it in a line: there he is sovereign, but his dominion extends equally over all the earth.

From that dominion the duty of praise is inferred. Henry states the inference plainly — if all are under God's dominion, all must do him homage. Clarke gives the reason for calling on the angels: every man with a sense of God's goodness feels his own powers inadequate to the praise he ought to offer, and so calls on the holiest of men and the supreme angels to help him. Spurgeon says his work of praise grows upon his hands, and summons those who dwell nearer the throne than we have leave to climb: to him who gave angelic strength let all angelic strength be given. He notices what their obedience consists in — they hearken for further commands, obeying as much by reverent listening as by energetic action; yet even for this let them take no praise but render all to him who kept them what they are.

Who exactly is being addressed is not agreed. Clarke declines to settle it: we know almost nothing of the economy of the heavenly host, and cannot tell what difference there is between angels, powers, hosts and ministers — though he wonders whether those that excel in strength are a distinct order employed among the children of men. Ellicott finds three grades in the psalmist's thought: high angels around the throne, angelic powers such as winds and lightnings commissioned to do God's behests, and creation generally. Wesley takes the hosts for angels, titled from their vast numbers, mighty power and exquisite order, and the ministers for the highest sort of servants. Gill offers a third possibility: the sun, moon and stars; or the angels again, called hosts for their legions; or rather, since they seem distinguished from the angels just addressed, the church militant, an army of volunteers under the Captain of their salvation. At the last verse he divides the same way, allowing all creatures but preferring regenerate persons. Ellicott keeps the wider sense and adds that the psalmist cannot remain silent but must repeat the self-dedication with which he began.
